claims.text: The initial system is a single-crystal FeNiCrCoCu coating on a single-crystal Cu matrix.
The initial coating is perfectly crystalline and contains no pre-existing defects.
The proposed simulations use 30 Å indentation depth and 10 m/s indentation velocity at 300, 600, 900, and 1200 K.
Above 900 K, thermally activated stacking-fault annihilation precedes localized interfacial amorphization.
The friction spike and loss of wear resistance above 900 K are caused by localized amorphization rather than ordinary softening of a crystalline lattice.
An amorphous layer forms transiently at the contact interface.
Annihilation of Shockley partial dislocations and collapse of stacking faults mediate formation of the amorphous layer.
Above 900 K, thermal energy exceeds the relevant stacking-fault energy barrier.
Crossing this barrier causes rapid annihilation of Shockley partial dislocations and dislocation starvation.
Dislocation starvation destabilizes the lattice and triggers a localized FCC-to-amorphous transformation.
The amorphous layer has high shear compliance and low yield strength.
High shear compliance and low yield strength increase the real contact area and cause a friction spike.
The amorphous layer lacks strain-hardening capacity, causing rapid material removal and loss of wear resistance.
Friction and wear increase sharply between 900 K and 1200 K.
The sharp increase in friction and wear coincides with a drop in FCC atom fraction and a spike in amorphous atom fraction in the contact zone.
The baseline response is a linear decrease in elastic modulus and hardness with increasing temperature, without a phase change or friction spike.
At 30 Å indentation depth, surface-to-volume effects dominate the response.
The Cu matrix remains elastic and does not contribute to the plastic deformation zone.
Changing the interatomic potential or strain rate may shift the temperature threshold for amorphization.
Increasing the stacking-fault energy barrier or imposing a crystalline constraint would suppress amorphous-structure formation.

contradictions.description: The protocol specifies normal nanoindentation but no lateral sliding or scratching motion, whereas the mechanism invokes a sliding interface and the measurements require a lateral force to define a coefficient of friction.

The hypothesis predicts that amorphization is required for the friction spike, but the first falsification condition treats the absence of a friction spike when the amorphous fraction remains low as falsifying; that outcome is instead compatible with the proposed mediator being absent.

The baseline asserts a linear decrease in modulus and hardness over increasing temperature, while the broader setup motivating the prediction includes an anomalous modulus increase at 600 K; the hypothesis does not reconcile that non-monotonic lower-temperature behavior with its stated baseline.
